summary: Defines the algorithms that must be implemented in IKEv2, so there is always at least one choice all implementations share. It also lists algorithms that should be implemented because they may be required in the future. It is a standards-track document that was later replaced by RFC 8247.

eli5.summary: Two machines need a few secret methods in common. This memo lists the ones every IKEv2 product must know.

subtitle: The encryption and hashing methods all IKEv2 implementations must support.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 can negotiate many different encryption algorithms, but without a common set, two implementations might share no algorithms and fail to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists which algorithms every implementation MUST support (such as 3DES-CBC and HMAC-SHA1), which SHOULD be supported because they may become mandatory later, and which MAY be supported.
tldr.outcome: This document was later replaced by RFC 8247 as cryptographic standards evolved.

today: RFC 4307 was later replaced by RFC 8247, which updated the algorithm requirements as cryptography evolved.

sections.title: Why Mandatory Algorithms Matter
sections.content: The Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2) protocol lets two systems negotiate which cryptographic algorithms to use for securing their communication. Different implementations may support different sets of algorithms. To ensure that any two implementations can negotiate and interoperate, the IETF must define a set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms—ones that every implementation MUST support. This document defines those algorithms and others that implementations SHOULD support because they may become mandatory in future versions.
sections.eli5: When two apps talk securely, they both need to know the same secret code. This memo lists the codes everyone must learn.

sections.title: Algorithm Status Levels
sections.content: The RFC uses several status labels. MUST algorithms must be implemented by all conforming implementations. SHOULD+ algorithms are likely to be promoted to MUST in the future and should be implemented now so they work widely when that happens. SHOULD- algorithms may be deprecated to MAY in future versions. MUST- algorithms are currently mandatory but expected to eventually become optional as cryptography evolves.
sections.eli5: Some codes are mandatory (everyone must know them). Some will probably become mandatory soon. Some might disappear. This tells you which is which.

sections.title: IKEv2 Mandatory and Recommended Algorithms
sections.content: For encrypted payloads, implementations MUST- implement 3DES-CBC for confidentiality and HMAC-SHA1 for integrity. AES-128-CBC is SHOULD+ for confidentiality. For key exchange, Group 2 (1024-bit MODP) is MUST-, while Group 14 (2048-bit MODP) is SHOULD+. For encryption transforms, 3DES is MUST-, AES-CBC is SHOULD+, and AES-CTR is SHOULD. For pseudo-random functions, HMAC-SHA1 is MUST, while AES128-CBC PRF is SHOULD+. For integrity (Transform Type 3), HMAC-SHA1-96 is MUST and AES-XCBC-96 is SHOULD+.
sections.eli5: Here are the methods: everyone must use these three (3DES, SHA1, and Group 2). Try to use these newer ones too (AES and bigger groups) because they will probably become required.

sections.title: Security and Future Changes
sections.content: The security of cryptographic systems depends on both algorithm strength and key length. Algorithms considered strong today may be broken tomorrow. The algorithms listed as MUST or SHOULD in this document are not known to be broken at the time of writing, but the RFC acknowledges that new revisions will be needed over time as cryptography evolves. Implementers should expect this document to be updated periodically to reflect the current best practice.
sections.eli5: These codes are safe today, but they might not be forever. New rules will come out when computers get faster or mathematicians find tricks.
